hook.line: La Candelaria is full of old things: old houses, old radios, old regulars. English says old for all of them; Spanish picks a different word for each, and picking wrong can be rude.
hook.en: La Candelaria has old historic houses.

examples.es: La radio de Rosa es muy antigua.

rule:
Spanish chooses its old by what is old.

*mayor*: people, said kindly. *Un señor mayor*, *mi abuela ya es mayor*. Never for things.
*viejo*: things that are worn out: *un carro viejo*, *este celular está muy viejo*. For a person it can sound blunt.
*antiguo*: things with history: *una casa antigua*, *una radio antigua*.

Put *antiguo* before the noun and it means former: *mi antiguo jefe* is the boss you used to have, whatever his age.
smallPrint: In Colombia *mi viejo* and *mi vieja* are an affectionate way to say my dad and my mum. Recognise it; don't try it on Don Hernando.

options: My old historic house was small.
This car is very worn out.
This car is a valuable antique.

readAndPick.es: Los cuadros de Rosa son antiguos.
options: Rosa's pictures are old and have history.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *Hernando es un señor ___.* (*viejo* or *mayor*) Hernando is an older gentleman, said kindly.
yourTurn.why: For people, *mayor* is the respectful word.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick and type the whole sentence: *La Candelaria tiene casas ___.* (*mayores* or *antiguas*) La Candelaria has old historic houses.
yourTurn.why: Houses with history are *antiguas*; *mayor* is never for things.

yourTurn.prompt: This phone is really old. (It's worn out.)

yourTurn.why: A building with history is *antiguo*, after the noun.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it kindly: *Mi abuelo es viejo.*
yourTurn.why: *Viejo* can sound blunt about a person; *mayor* is kind.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it plural: *El edificio es antiguo.*

pitfalls.wrong: La radio de Rosa es mayor.
pitfalls.right: La radio de Rosa es antigua.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Mayor* is only for people; an old radio with history is *antigua*.
*Viejo* can sound rude about a person; *mayor* says the same thing kindly.
For former, *antiguo* goes before the noun.

personal: Describe two old things in your life: something worn out (*viejo*) and something with history (*antiguo*). Then mention an older person you know, kindly, with *mayor*.
